1 PROJECT DETAILS
1.1 Summary Description of the Project
The project activity facilitates the transition of smallholder farming systems toward
sustainable and climate-resilient agricultural practices. Core interventions include reduced
or zero tillage, incorporation of cover crops, and the replacement of synthetic fertilizers with
organic nutrient inputs. These practices are designed to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG)
emissions—specifically carbon dioxide (CO₂), methane (CH₄), and nitrous oxide (N₂O)—
while enhancing atmospheric carbon removal through increased Soil Organic Carbon (SOC)
sequestration. Through improved residue management, elevated biomass inputs, and
reduced soil disturbance, the project simultaneously supports climate change mitigation and
the long-term enhancement of soil fertility.
Developed by Asvata, the initiative is structured as a grouped project under the VM0042 v2.0
methodology (Methodology for Improved Agricultural Land Management), with a total
potential implementation area of 20,000 hectares. This grouped approach allows for the
phased inclusion of additional project activity instances over time. Crop selection—including
cotton and other regionally relevant species—is tailored to agro ecological conditions and
local agronomic practices to optimize both mitigation outcomes and farmer co-benefits.
To date, the project has enrolled 1,499 smallholder farmers managing a cumulative area of
2,222 hectares in and around Nagpur, Maharashtra, for implementation of improved
Agricultural Land Management (ALM) practices. Baseline assessments indicate that
approximately 80% of participating farmers previously practiced monoculture cotton
cultivation, often followed by extended fallow periods. The remaining 20% engaged in short-
duration cereal or wheat cropping. Conventional practices prevalent across the baseline
scenario included high-intensity tillage and synthetic fertilizer application, both of which
contribute to GHG emissions and soil degradation.
The transition to regenerative practices under this project is expected to improve soil
biophysical properties, enhance productivity, and strengthen resilience to climatic variability.
Emission reductions and removals are rigorously quantified and monitored in accordance
with the methodological framework of VM0042, ensuring environmental integrity and
verifiability. The project targets a cumulative mitigation potential of approximately 1,951,250
tCO₂e over a 30-year crediting period.
During the first monitoring period, spanning June 7, 2022, to April 30, 2025, the project was
operational across 5,000 hectares, resulting in verified GHG mitigation outcomes totaling
119,583 tCO₂e.
This project represents an integrated approach to sustainable land management, delivering
quantifiable climate benefits while promoting livelihood resilience among smallholder
communities in Maharashtra and Telangana. It contributes meaningfully to national and
global climate targets by mainstreaming regenerative agriculture practices at scale.

1.4 Project Eligibility
General eligibility
The project activity is within the VCS Program's scope. The project reduces the greenhouse
gases (GHGs) listed in the Kyoto Protocol, including CO2, CH4, and N2O from agricultural
residue management, as well as N2O from fertiliser reduction. The project adheres to the
Improved Land Management (VM0042 v2.1) Methodology. The agricultural land
management (ALM) approach offers methods for calculating the removals and reductions of
greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions (CO2, CH4, and N2O) brought about by the
implementation of improved ALM practices.
Project eligibility according to the scope listed in section 2.1.1 in VCS Standard v4.7

Furthermore, the project is suitable under the terms of the VCS Programme because it

AFOLU projects are expected to start the pipeline listing procedure within three years from
the project start date, according section 3.8.2 of VCS standard v4.7. The project start date
is 7th June-2022, and the three-year period is until 7th June 2025 before the listing of the
project document has been completed with VERRA.
The VM0042 Methodology is applicable to a wide range of project activities that, in
comparison to the baseline scenario, improve SOC storage and/or decrease net emissions
of CO2, CH4, and N2O from ALM operations. Since the project activity involves increasing
SOC storage and lowering net emissions of CO2, CH4, and N2O, it complies with the
methodology.
AFOLU project eligibility
• The Project is an Agricultural Land Management (ALM) project, which is an eligible AFOLU
project category in line with Appendix 1, VCS Standard 4.7. The Project is an eligible ALM
project as it includes Improved Cropland Management activities that reduce and sequester
net GHG emissions of cropland systems.
• The Project focuses on increasing soil organic carbon (SOC) storage in annual cropping
systems through the implementation of regenerative agricultural practices as well as
reducing net emissions of carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4) and nitrogen (N2O) through
activities which improve the efficiency of fertiliser use. The Project activities follow the
eligibility criteria laid out by the VM0042 Improved Agricultural Land Management version
2.1 approved by Verra on 11 sept 2024 (hereafter referred to as “VM0042”)
• The area where the Project activities occur has not been cleared, converted or degraded
of native ecosystems throughout the 10-years prior to the project start date and does not

Page 7

occur on a wetland. This will be assessed using GIS technology for each field submitted
for verification and proof of this will be presented in the monitoring reports. This is a
voluntary Project, meaning that the emission reductions and sequestration would not have
taken place in the absence of the Project.
Transfer project eligibility
The project activity is not a transfer project and not seeking CPAs registration. Hence this
section is not applicable.
1.5 Project Design
Indicate if the project has been designed as:
☐ Single location or installation
☐ Multiple locations or project activity instances (but not a grouped project)
☒ Grouped project
Grouped Project Design
Grouped projects are structured in such a way that they allow for project expansion in the
phases following subsequent project validation. Based on the assumption that an increasing
number of project activity instances (fields) will be adopting a set of eligible ALM practices
and get enrolled in this project as the project expands within the defined project boundary.
This means that this project will include further project activity instances (fields) during the
subsequent validation/ verification phases of the project Validation will be based upon initial
project activity instances located within the project area. The eligibility criteria for the
inclusion of new project instances will comply with VCS Standard v4.7, and the VM0042
methodology criteria listed below.
Eligibility Criteria
The project instances will be eligible for inclusion in this grouped project as they meet
eligibility criteria set out in 3.6.16- 3.6.17 of the VCS Standard v4.7 as described in table 1
below:

1.8 Ownership
The lands utilized for implementing the VCS project activity are legally owned by small and
marginal farmers. These lands are under the implementation control of the Project Proponent
(PP) through an agreement signed between the smallholder farmers and the PP at the start
date of the VCS project activity, and are expected to remain under such control throughout
the crediting period. This agreement complies with the VCS Standard Version 4.7, paragraph
3.7.1, point 6.
Additionally, as the rightful owners of their respective farmlands, the farmers have the
authority to grant RPGF overall control and responsibility for the Improved Agricultural Land
Management Project, as the Project Proponent, without infringing upon their rights. Each
participating farmer formally assigns their carbon rights to RPGF through a signed
agreement, which are subsequently transferred to ASVATA. The revenue generated from the
sale of carbon offsets will be distributed among stakeholders in accordance with the policies
and decisions set by ASVATA’s management.
Supporting evidence of project ownership, such as MOUs, agreement documents, and land
ownership records, are held by the Project Proponent and can be provided to the
Validation/Verification Body upon request.

i.e., farmer engagement took place.

1.12 Description of the Project Activity
RPGF Group, actively promotes regenerative and sustainable farming practices among
farmers. These practices include, but are not limited to, crop rotation, crop residue
management, improved land and nutrient management techniques—such as balancing the
application of organic and inorganic nitrogen fertilizers. The specific practices implemented
under this initiative are outlined below:
A. Crop Rotation
i. Under baseline conditions (non-project farmers), over 80% of cotton farmers engage
in monocropping. Typically, after harvesting cotton in January or February, fields are
left fallow for approximately nine months, from March through May.

Page 13
VCS Joint Project Description & Monitoring Report Template, v4.4
13
ii. In contrast, farmers participating in the IALM project utilize their land throughout the
year by adopting cotton-wheat or cotton-bengal gram cropping sequences. This
ensures continuous crop cover across all seasons.
B. Improved Tillage Practices
Adoption of improved tillage methods enhances soil structure by minimizing compaction and
erosion, increasing soil carbon sequestration, and maintaining or improving soil fertility.
These practices support the accumulation of organic matter and stimulate microbial activity,
thereby improving nutrient cycling and leading to more stable and higher crop yields.
i. Traditionally, most cotton farmers in the Nagpur district performed deep ploughing
(over 30 cm) annually, followed by one or two harrowing operations using cultivators
and rotavators. These tillage activities typically occurred between the second week
of May and the end of the month.
ii. Farmers associated with ASVATA, within the same geographical area, have adopted
regenerative tillage practices. These farmers now conduct shallow tillage (<15 cm)
only once every two to three years, followed by one or two harrowing passes during
cotton cultivation. Tillage operations are usually carried out from the end of April to
mid-June. On average, primary tillage depth ranges from 10–15 cm, while secondary
tillage is between 6–8 cm. Additionally, approximately 30–40% of these farmers now
use bullock-drawn implements for field preparation.
C. Reduced Use of Synthetic Fertilizers
RPG farmers have fully transitioned away from inorganic fertilizers in cotton cultivation,
relying entirely on organic inputs. Most organic farmers utilize Farm Yard Manure (FYM),
vermicompost, Jeevamrutha, biofertilizers, and green manures. Maintaining and gradually
improving soil fertility is essential for achieving economically viable yields. To produce
organic cotton, it is crucial to enhance and sustain the organic matter content of the soil,
thereby improving its physical properties, structure, and nutrient availability. Given the limited
availability of large quantities of FYM, combining different sources with diverse biological
properties is recommended to meet crop nutrient demands effectively.
D. Crop Residue Management
Conventional farmers typically remove and burn cotton stalks immediately after harvest. In
contrast, program farmers leave cotton stalks in the field post-harvest to prevent soil erosion
caused by wind and rain. These residues are either incorporated into the soil using rotavators
or are uprooted and converted into biochar or compost. The estimated quantity of cotton
plant residue is approximately 2.7 tons per hectare.

1.14 Conditions Prior to Project Initiation
• Ecosystem type: The ecosystem type before the project initiation was terrestrial
ecosystem with land classified as agricultural lands.
• Current and historical land-use: The chosen project sites have a historical background
of being utilized for agricultural purposes. To validate that the project locations are indeed
agricultural or croplands, a Land Use Land Cover (LULC) map will be created for the
project area. This map will serve as evidence of the land's agricultural nature.
• Climatic conditions: Maharashtra has typical monsoon climate, with hot, rainy and cold
weather seasons. Tropical conditions prevail all over the state, and even the hill stations
are not that cold. Dew, frost, hail can also be happened sometimes according to the
seasonal weather2
a. Summer: March, April and May are the hottest months. During April and May
thunderstorms are common all over the state. Temperature varies between
22°C-39°C during this season.
2 https://www.maharashtratourism.net/climate.html#google_vignette

Page 15
VCS Joint Project Description & Monitoring Report Template, v4.4
15
b. Rainy: Rainfall starts normally in the first week of June. July is the wettest month
in Maharashtra, while August too gets substantial rain. Monsoon starts its retreat
with the coming of September from the state.
c. Winter: Cool dry spell, with clear skies gentle breeze and pleasant weather
prevails from November to February. But the eastern part of Maharashtra
sometimes receives some rainfall. Temperature varies between 12°C-34°C
during this season.
d. Rainfall: Rainfall in Maharashtra differs from region to region. Thane, Raigad,
Ratnagiri and Sindhudurg districts, receive heavy rains of an average of 200
centimeters annually. But the districts of Nasik, Pune, Ahmednagar, Dhule,
Jalgaon, Satara, Sangli, Solapur and parts of Kolhapur get rainfall less than 50
centimeters. Rainfall particularly concentrates to the Konkan and Sahyadrian
Maharashtra. Central Maharashtra receives less rainfall. However, under the
influence of the Bay of Bengal, eastern Vidarbha receives good rainfall in July,
August and September.
• Hydrology: In central India, groundwater is a primary source of drinking water and
supports more than 70–80% of the water demand for agriculture. Groundwater
resources are heavily dependent on the Indian summer monsoon (June–
September), as 90% of the annual rainfall receives only during the monsoon season
and 10% of the annual rainfall in the remaining seasons of the year. Groundwater
resources in the northern region of central India become more vulnerable due to a
deficit in monsoon rainfall3.
• Soil type and Health: India exhibits a diverse range of soil types, reflecting its varied
geography and climate. The most prevalent soil types appear to be alluvial soils,
black soils, and red soils, which are found in significant quantities across multiple
states. Alluvial soils are particularly dominant in the northern plains, with Uttar
Pradesh having the largest area (23,089.58 Ha) covered by alluvial soils. Other
states with substantial alluvial soil coverage include Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Punjab,
and West Bengal. This is consistent with the presence of major river systems like the
Ganges and its tributaries in these regions. Black soils, often associated with cotton-
growing regions, are most prominent in Maharashtra (15,423.78 Ha) and Madhya
Pradesh (15,203.57 Ha). These soils are also found in significant amounts in Gujarat,
Karnataka, and Andhra Pradesh, indicating their prevalence in central and western
India. Red soils cover large areas in several states, with Madhya Pradesh (16,601.28
Ha) and Andhra Pradesh (9,930.11 Ha) having the most extensive coverage. These
3 https://www.mdpi.com/2306-
5338/9/12/222#:~:text=In%20central%20India%2C%20groundwater%20is,extraction%20%5B23%2C28%5D.

Page 16
VCS Joint Project Description & Monitoring Report Template, v4.4
16
soils are also common in Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, and Odisha, suggesting their
prevalence in peninsular India4.
1.15 Compliance with Laws, Statutes and Other Regulatory Frameworks
India does not regulate GHG emissions from agriculture in the smallholder farming systems.
By adhering to following laws and regulations, the project will demonstrate its commitment
to promoting sustainable agriculture practices while ensuring compliance with local, regional,
and national legal frameworks in the project area
• Fertilizer Control Order, 1985
• Seeds Bill, 2004
• Insecticide (Amendment) Act, 2000
• Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers’ Rights Act, 2001
• Farmers & Farm Workers Commission Act, 2017
• Environment (Protection) Act, 1986
• Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981
• Water (Prevention & Control of Pollution) Act, 1974
• National Biodiversity Act, 2002: Compliance with this act is ensured by promoting
regenerative practices that conserve biodiversity by minimizes agrochemical use
hence increase soil diversity.
• Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981: Compliance with this act will be
ensured by implementing practices that reduce air pollution associated with
agricultural activities, such as promoting the avoidance of burning crop residues.
• Water (Prevention & Control of Pollution) Act, 1974: The project's regenerative
practices, including fertigation and reduced tillage, prevent water pollution and
promote water conservation. It ensures compliance with regulations for water quality
protection by minimizing nutrient runoff and soil erosion.
• Environment (Protection) Act, 1986: The project ensures compliance with this act by
implementing environmentally sustainable practices and minimizing adverse impacts
on the environment. This includes adhering to regulations related to air and water
quality waste management, and environmental pollution. The project promotes

1.18 Sustainable Development Contributions
Sustainable Development Contributions Activity Description
SDG SDG Impact
The adoption of advanced regenerative agricultural
practices promotes increased crop productivity and
economic well-being, empowering individuals to achieve
a sustainable livelihood. Through the use of effective
methods, both the quality and quantity of agricultural
output are enhanced, helping to ensure adequate food
availability for all.
This project aligns with the SDG target 4.3 by providing
vocational trainings to the individuals associated with the
project activity. By engaging individuals from local
communities, the initiative promotes equal access to
education and technical skills needed for effective
participation in ALM activities.
Unsustainable agricultural practices which affect the
productivity of land, which in turn affect the quality and
the quantity of the produce. Due to this, a large section of
farmers is heavily affected, and it is more pronounced for
the small and marginal farmers. Often the only source of
income for these farmers/landowners is agriculture,
making them vulnerable to poverty in case of crop failure.
This implementation of project activities will create job
opportunities and support regional development by
providing training and employment in rural areas.

Page 19
VCS Joint Project Description & Monitoring Report Template, v4.4
19
The project activity involves the implementation of ALM
activities over an area of 2,200 ha across the project
boundary. This plantation activity will help in the
reduction/removal of net GHG emissions from the
atmosphere and the addition of more oxygen into the
surrounding environment, thus creating a clean
environment. An estimated total 225,533 tCO2e will be
removed during a crediting period of 30 years. Therefore,
the project activity will promote climate mitigation and
adaptation strategies.
The ALM activities will promote various ecosystem
services including improvement of the microclimate of the
area, conservation of soil by reducing soil erosion,
enhancing ground water quality & quantity, and
increasing soil health of the project area.
NITI Aayog is the central institution responsible for driving the attainment of SDGs in
India, spearheading the 2030 Agenda through a collaborative and competitive approach
among states. The organization works rigorously to monitor all the 17 Goals over 100
indicators nationwide.

1.19 Additional Information Relevant to the Project
Leakage Management
The aim of the project is to increase organic input from farmyard manure, compost to
increase soil nutrient and soil carbon. The crop residue produced after harvest is
integrated into the soil.
The possible source of leakage could be increase of fuel wood and grazing activity
outside the project boundary due to decrease in supply for fodder and fuel for cooking.
However, the cropland in the project area do not allow grazing in any time of the year.
Therefore, there was no displacement of pre-project grazing activities.
Commercially Sensitive Information
No commercially sensitive information has been excluded from the public version of the
project description
Further Information
No further information is added.

Stakeholder diversity and
changes over time
The local stakeholder group comprises farmers and
landowners within the project area where local
consultations are conducted. Below is a delineation of the
diversity within each stakeholder category along with
potential shifts in their composition over time.
• Small holder farmers: Predominantly rural-based,
these stakeholders are deeply entrenched in
agricultural activities, forming the backbone of the local
economy. Their livelihoods depend on the performance
of crop and livestock markets, rendering their income
subject to fluctuations influenced by climatic conditions,
market trends, and governmental policies. The lifestyle
of farmers and landowners varies significantly based
on factors such as farm size, agricultural practices
adopted, and access to resources. These disparities
shape their perspectives and priorities concerning the
project.
• Community members: The community comprises
individuals with strong ties to rural livelihoods,
underscoring their affinity for agrarian activities and
traditional practices. They exhibit a mosaic of social,
economic, and cultural backgrounds, contributing to
the vibrancy and heterogeneity of the local population.
Economic diversity is evident within the community,
with disparities in income levels, employment
opportunities, and access to resources shaping
individual experiences and aspirations. Cultural norms,
traditions, and values prevalent within the community
influence stakeholder interactions, perceptions of the
project, and decision-making processes.
• Local Policymakers: The local policymakers have
authority and influence in shaping agricultural policies
and developmental initiatives. Their work often
revolves around agricultural issues, positioning them
as crucial intermediaries between governmental
bodies and grassroots stakeholders.
• Non-Governmental Organizations (NGOs): NGO
employees typically specialize in areas related to
agriculture, championing causes aligned with
sustainable farming practices, rural development, or

Page 26
VCS Joint Project Description & Monitoring Report Template, v4.4
26
environmental conservation. These stakeholders are
driven by a shared commitment to effecting positive
change within the agricultural landscape. NGOs play a
pivotal role in amplifying the voices of marginalized
stakeholders, providing technical expertise, and
facilitating community engagement initiatives.
• Employees: They are employed by the PP, These
stakeholders contribute to the operational and logistical
facets of agricultural endeavors. They plays an
important role in connecting stakeholders to the project
and are important for stakeholder engagement.
• Universities/Research Institutes: This additional
stakeholder category encompasses individuals
engaged in academia or pursuing education within
institute/university settings. Their focus on scientific
research related to agriculture brings a specialized
perspective to the stakeholder landscape.
Interactions among these diverse stakeholder groups
further enrich the dialogue surrounding the project's
objectives and implementation strategies. These
stakeholder groups are expected to stay made up of a
similar make-up in the future.
Expected changes in well-being The stakeholders most likely to be impacted by the project
are smallholder’s farmers of the project area. As provided
in the section 1.12, it is expected that the project relative
to baseline scenario will have positive impact on the
environment such as:
• Increase carbon sequestration in the soil and
therewith improved soil quality.
• Reduced erosion and improved soil quality.
• Increased resilience to extreme weather events
such as droughts and flooding.
• Improved water retention in the soil, less runoff and
• Reducing pollution of water bodies creating
improved water quality.
• Improved biodiversity such as increased
development of micro-organisms, strengthening of
ecosystems.
• Reduced pollutants in the soil, air and water, due to
the reduced use of chemical fertilisers
Moreover, the project provides the following co benefits
such as:
• Knowledge and skill enhancement: Farmers will gain
awareness of sustainable agricultural methods

Page 27
VCS Joint Project Description & Monitoring Report Template, v4.4
27
through training sessions conducted by the project
partners (PP), fostering local skill development.
• Income boost: Farmer livelihoods will improve as they
earn additional income through carbon credits.
• Encouragement for young farmers: The project aims
to motivate the younger generation to remain in or
engage with farming activities.
• Potential for both direct and indirect employment
opportunities on farms.
Location of stakeholders All identified stakeholder groups, as outlined in the table
above, were actively encouraged to participate in the
consultation process conducted within the project areas of
Maharashtra and Telangana It is anticipated that local
communities, and customary rights holders will not be
affected by the project
Location of resources The project will encompass project activity instances
location in the states of Maharashtra and Telangana.

The aim of the stakeholder consultation is to meaningfully

Ongoing communication Ongoing conversations are kept open, via email,
WhatsApp, and phone calls in addition to in-person
meetings where applicable, such that project
stakeholders can always reach a project proponent
representative
Stakeholder input All valuable discussions and inputs from stakeholders
who participated in the consultation meetings were
carefully documented and integrated into various sections
of this PD. Common feedback, such as inquiries
regarding training and guidance on carbon farming, as
well as local agronomic advice, was raised by the farmers.
In response, the project is actively addressing these
concerns by organizing continuous training sessions.
Additionally, regular awareness meetings are being
conducted at the village level to emphasize the
significance of regenerative agriculture and highlight
carbon as a co-benefit, encouraging farmers to adopt
these practices.

VCS Joint Project Description & Monitoring Report Template, v4.4

Free Prior and Informed Consent
Obtaining consent The principle of Free, Prior, and Informed Consent (FPIC)
ensures that farmers have the right to self-determination
and to give or withhold consent to projects affecting their
ancestral domains, lands, territories, and resources. It is a
fundamental process for recognizing farmer’s rights,
building trust, and legitimizing project presence in areas
with cultural, spiritual, and territorial significance.
FPIC was secured at the initiation of the carbon project
development by the farmer communities within the project
area. Comprehensive details about the planned project
activities, involvement of farmers, expected outcomes,
benefits and co-benefits and potential risks associated
with the project were provided by the PP to the
communities. FPIC survey forms were signed by
representatives of the communities.
Outcome of FPIC Apart from the farmers, there are no customary right
holders of the land nor are there any indigenous people or
other local community members who hold the authority to
determine or consent to the activities conducted on the
land that is part of this Project.
Grievance Redress Procedure
Development process The feedback and grievance redressal mechanism has
the following objectives:
• To inform decision making related to project design
and development, integrating feedback into the
project.
• To serve as a mechanism for timely resolution of a
problem and prevent problems from escalating into
social conflict.
• To be part of the project monitoring and evaluation
process and contribute to learnings.
Grievance redress procedure The project proponent ensures that a structured
mechanism is in place to address stakeholder disputes
during project planning and implementation. A complaint
register is maintained at the project office for farmers to
record their concerns and all registered grievances are
reviewed and resolved in a timely manner. Farmers can
also directly contact the PP team via phone for support

Page 30
VCS Joint Project Description & Monitoring Report Template, v4.4
30
during project implementation, and any concerns raised
are recorded and addressed promptly.
Public Comments
Public comments are to be addressed in the Final PD.

Benefit Sharing
Process used to design the
benefit sharing plan
The benefit-sharing plan is designed to allocate a
significant portion of the revenue from carbon credit sales
to participant farmers, enhancing their livelihoods and
improving the surrounding environment. The remaining
revenue is designated to cover project development and
management costs for Asvata.
Summary of the benefit sharing
plan
The Landowner will receive incentives in accordance with
the mutually agreed terms, contingent upon the Project
Proponent’s successful generation of carbon revenue
following the project’s validation and registration under
the Verified Carbon Standard (VCS).
Approval and dissemination of
benefit sharing plan
The benefit sharing mechanism has been agreed upon
after due consultations among the project participants
and approved by the project management.
The benefit sharing plan is duly mentioned in the
agreement made among the participant farmer, and
ASVATA, and disseminated to the farmers participated in

Rare, Threatened, and Endangered species
Is the project located in or adjacent to habitats for rare, threatened, or endangered species?
☐ Yes ☒ No
Introduction of species
Not applicable as the project does not involve the introduction of any invasive species into
the project area. The crop varieties utilized by farmers are regionally accepted, and the
project activities strictly adhere to this principle. Neither do any of the project activities allow
any invasive species to thrive through project implementation. The different crop varieties
reported by farmers in the project area will be duly recorded, particularly for cotton.
Ecosystem conversion
The Project does not clear or drain existing natural ecosystems and has not done so in at
least the 10 years prior to the project start date. For each project instance, a GIS check will
be done to confirm that the project area has not been cleared of natural ecosystems in the
past 10 years and is not located on a wetland, peatland, or forest.

3.4 Baseline Scenario
As per VM0042 v2.0 methodology, continuation of pre-project agricultural management
practices is the most plausible baseline scenario. The conventional agriculture practices in
baseline scenario of the project area includes practices such as:
1. Excessive fertiliser application through broadcasting
2. Burning of crop residue
3. Intensive tillage practice

Page 37
VCS Joint Project Description & Monitoring Report Template, v4.4
37
The baseline scenario is determined for each sample unit (e.g. for each field) by applying a
historical look-back period to produce an annual schedule of activities to be repeated over
the first crediting period. This is determined via the collection of information pertaining to
reduced fertilizer use, water management, reduced tillage, crop residue management and
avoidance of burning practices during the three-year period immediately before the project
start date. Information relating to agricultural management activities was sourced via farmer
signed attestation, survey and remote sensing analysis.
3.5 Additionality
Regulatory Surplus
Is the project registered or seeking registration in an UNFCCC Annex 1 or Non-Annex 1 country?
☐ Annex 1 country ☒ Non-Annex 1 country
Are the project activities mandated by any law, statute, or other regulatory framework?
☐ Yes ☒ No
If the project is located inside a Non-Annex 1 country and the project activities are mandated by
a law, statute, or other regulatory framework, are such laws, statutes, or regulatory frameworks
systematically enforced?
☐ Yes ☒ No
If no, describe which mandated laws, statutes, or other regulatory frameworks require project
activities and provide evidence of systematic non-enforcement to demonstrate regulatory
surplus.
Additionality Methods
As per the latest version of the VCS Standard, section 3.14.1 and methodology VM0042
v2.1 requirements, the additionality of this project is demonstrated in two steps:
1. The project shall demonstrate regulatory surplus at validation and each project
crediting period renewal.
a. Regularity surplus
b. Barrier analysis
c. Common practice analysis
2. Additionality shall be demonstrated and assessed in accordance with the
requirements set out in the methodology applied to the project.
3.6 Methodology Deviations
Not applicable. There is no methodology deviation.

4 IMPLEMENTATION STATUS
4.1 Implementation Status of the Project Activity
For all projects, describe the implementation status of the project activity(s), including
information on the following:
• The operation of the project activity(s) during the monitoring period, including any
information on events that may impact the GHG emission reductions or removals and
monitoring.
• Any other changes (e.g., to project proponent or other entities).
For AFOLU projects, include information on the following:
• Where no new project activities have been implemented during the current monitoring
period, demonstrate that previously implemented project activities continued to be
implemented during the current monitoring period.
• Report any loss of carbon stock that occurred during the monitoring period. The date of the
loss(es), date of discovery(s), size (hectares impacted) and extent (tCO2e) of the loss must
be described. Specify if the loss meets the definition of a loss event and/or reversal. In all
cases, justify how the project meets VCS requirements related to loss events and reversals.
